column1: Measuring Firm-Level Inflation Exposure: A Deep Learning Approach

The thesis titled A Deep Learning Approach for Computations of Exposure Profiles for High-Dimensional Bermudan Options by Kristoffer Andersson and Cornelis W. Oosterlee presents a novel method for approximating expected exposures and potential future exposures of Bermudan options using neural networks. The approach is divided into two phases. Initially  the Deep Optimal Stopping (DOS) algorithm is employed to learn the optimal stopping rule from Monte-Carlo samples of underlying risk factors. This learned strategy is then applied to new realizations to create cashflow paths. In the second phase  these paths are projected onto risk factors to approximate pathwise option values  with regression performed using both ordinary least squares and neural networks  the latter providing more accurate results.

The expected exposure is defined in terms of cashflow paths and pathwise option values  with a simple Monte-Carlo average yielding accurate approximations. Potential future exposure is estimated using the empirical α-percentile. The study demonstrates that both expected and potential future exposures can be computed under either the risk-neutral or real-world measure without retraining the neural networks.

The thesis is structured as follows: an introduction to the problem  a detailed problem formulation including Bermudan options and exposure profiles  a section on learning stopping decisions using the DOS algorithm  and proposed adjustments to the algorithm. It also covers learning pathwise option values through regression  approximation algorithms for exposure profiles  and numerical results using Black-Scholes and Heston model dynamics. The results show the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to traditional Monte-Carlo-based algorithms  highlighting the advantages of neural network regression over ordinary least squares in approximating pathwise option values.

The introduction emphasizes the importance of accurately computing financial exposures  particularly for options with early-exercise features like Bermudan options. The thesis addresses the challenge of approximating both the option value and the stopping decision  crucial for calculating expected and potential future exposures. The proposed method is validated through numerical experiments  demonstrating its accuracy and efficiency in high-dimensional settings.
